about.title: Goleta Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Goleta residents rely on a mix of local clinics and nearby Santa Barbara County hospitals for everything from routine care to surgery, and most visits go fine. But when a provider misses a diagnosis, makes a surgical error, or mishandles medication, the consequences can follow a patient for years. California's MICRA law sets specific rules for these cases, including short notice windows and a requirement for qualified medical expert review, which makes early guidance important. Our team handles medical malpractice claims for Goleta residents who believe they were harmed by substandard medical care. We review your records, consult medical experts, and explain whether a claim may be viable. There's no cost for an initial consultation, and we work on contingency, meaning no fee unless there's a recovery. A bad outcome by itself isn't proof of malpractice, but if something feels wrong about the care you received, a conversation with us can help you understand your options.

items.title: Deadlines Are Shorter Than You'd Expect
items.desc: California generally gives one year from when you discover the harm, and no more than three years from the injury itself, plus a required 90-day notice before filing suit. Missing these windows can end a claim before it starts.

items.title: Expert Review Is Built Into the Process
items.desc: California law almost always requires a qualified medical expert to support a malpractice claim, so we can help arrange the right medical evaluation before proceeding.

items.title: Understanding the Non-Economic Damages Cap
items.desc: MICRA sets a cap on non-economic damages that adjusts upward each year, and we can walk you through how that cap may apply to your specific situation.

items.question: I had a poor outcome after treatment near Hollister Avenue in Goleta — is that automatically malpractice?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California law recognizes that medicine involves risk, and a bad outcome alone doesn't establish malpractice. What matters is whether the provider's care fell below the accepted standard, which is typically assessed with input from a qualified medical expert.

items.question: How long do I have to bring a claim in California?
items.answer: Generally, you have one year from when you discovered or reasonably should have discovered the injury, but no more than three years from the date it occurred. There's also a required 90-day notice period before a lawsuit can be filed, so earlier review matters.

items.question: Does it cost anything to contact you?
items.answer: No, an initial consultation is free. We typically work on contingency, meaning we only get paid if you recover compensation.
